scanner_findings.title: Directory server sets no per-connection read timeout or concurrency cap (hypothesis)
scanner_findings.prerequisites: The directory is reachable by anonymous clients with no proxy in front that enforces read timeouts or connection limits. The task says the proxy normally provides this, so the finding applies only when the proxy does not.
scanner_findings.impact: A client that opens many TCP connections and sends headers or a PUT body slowly, or not at all, can hold connection tasks open indefinitely. The only bound is the 4096-byte body limit, which caps size but not time or connection count, so this can exhaust tasks and file descriptors.
scanner_findings.evidence: serve_with_policy calls `let res = axum::serve(listener, router_with_policy(store, policy)).await;` with no timeout layer and no connection limit. The only limit in router_with_policy is `.layer(DefaultBodyLimit::max(MAX_RECORD_SIZE))`, which bounds size, not duration.
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Wrap the router in a timeout layer (for example tower-http TimeoutLayer or tower::timeout) and bound concurrent connections (for example a tower ConcurrencyLimitLayer or a semaphore around accept). Alternatively document that the proxy must enforce both and add a test that a stalled PUT is closed.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Run the directory without a proxy and open 1000 connections that send a partial PUT header or body and then stall. Measure whether the connections and tasks persist after 60 seconds, and check which header_read_timeout and body timeouts axum and hyper apply by default.

scanner_findings.title: Closed-network directory serves member records to anonymous readers
scanner_findings.prerequisites: A directory started with router_with_policy or serve_with_policy for a closed network. Any unauthenticated client that knows or guesses a member node ID.
scanner_findings.impact: The membership gate only guards writes. Anyone can fetch a member's signed record, which reveals the endpoint ID, direct IP addresses, relay URLs and all identities. Non-members can use this to learn the member roster and reach member endpoints, which a closed network is meant to prevent. Whether this is a real exposure depends on deployment and on whether the network treats its records as confidential.
scanner_findings.evidence: router_with_policy: .route("/v1/records", put(put_record)).route("/v1/records/{node_id}", get(get_record)) with the policy only in put_record: if let Some(p) = &dir.policy && let Err(e) = p.check_record(&rec, ...) => FORBIDDEN. get_record: match dir.store.resolve(&id) { Some(rec) => rec.to_bytes() ... }, with no policy or caller check.
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: If records of a closed network are confidential, require a membership proof on GET (for example a signed challenge from a member identity) or serve GET only on an internal listener. If public reads are intended, document that the roster is public and state it in the policy docs.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Demonstrated code behaviour: a GET with no credentials returns the stored record for a node ID under a policy router. Whether that is a defect depends on the intended confidentiality of closed-network records, which needs confirmation from the design docs and membership.rs.

scanner_findings.title: Membership is checked only on PUT, so revoked or expired certificates keep resolving until the record expires
scanner_findings.prerequisites: A directory with a membership policy. A member's record with a valid certificate is accepted, then the member is removed from the network or its certificate expires. Records last up to MAX_TTL (24 h) plus MAX_CLOCK_SKEW, and the store does not re-check membership.
scanner_findings.impact: After removal, the removed member's record can still be resolved through GET, and it stays there until the record expires. Removal is therefore delayed by up to about 24 hours, and a removed member can still be dialled through the directory during that window. The directory also keeps the record after its certificate has expired.
scanner_findings.evidence: put_record: if let Some(p) = &dir.policy && let Err(e) = p.check_record(&rec, std::time::SystemTime::now()) => FORBIDDEN; then dir.store.insert(&rec). store.rs resolve_at returns Some(rec.clone()) or Some(latest.clone()) after checking only expires_at and withdrawal, never the membership certificate. record.rs MAX_TTL = 24 h.
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Make resolve or GET re-run the membership check at read time, or have the directory prune records whose certificates are revoked or expired. Alternatively, bound the record expiry by the certificate's expiry when the record is stored.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Needs a test: create a valid member record under a policy, revoke or let the certificate expire, then GET it after the record's own expiry would be unreached. The result depends on what check_record and the certificate format enforce in membership.rs, which was not supplied, so the behaviour cannot be confirmed from these files alone.

scanner_findings.title: Identity signatures are over a bare 32-byte digest with no protocol tag, so a signature the same key makes for another protocol can be reused as a record signature
scanner_findings.prerequisites: The same secp256k1 identity key is used to sign arbitrary 32-byte prehashes in another protocol (the module doc says yagna identity::Sign and ya-relay challenge responses sign raw 32-byte values). An attacker can make the victim sign a chosen 32-byte value in that other protocol, and can choose a payload whose RECORD_DOMAIN-tagged SHA-256 digest equals that value. This is a hypothesis: the other protocol's exact inputs are not in the supplied source.
scanner_findings.impact: If it holds, the attacker obtains a valid identity signature over a record that binds the victim's identity to the attacker's own endpoint key, which has its own valid endpoint signature. The module's stated guarantee that no party can point an identity at a different endpoint would fail. The attack needs the victim to sign attacker-chosen digests in the other protocol.
scanner_findings.evidence: pub fn digest_of(payload: &[u8]) -> [u8; 32] { let mut h = Sha256::new(); h.update(RECORD_DOMAIN); h.update(payload); h.finalize().into() } and in verify_at: let digest = NodeRecord::digest_of(&wire.payload); ... sig.recover_node_id(&digest) with no per-purpose tag on the identity signature.
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Sign a domain-separated message that the other protocols cannot produce, for example an EIP-191-style prefix or a structured hash that starts with a tag no other protocol uses, and verify the identity signature over that. Alternatively, have identities sign only a digest computed with a per-purpose key that can never be a valid challenge in other protocols. Document that identity keys must not sign arbitrary prehashes.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Check the ya-relay challenge-response and yagna identity::Sign inputs. Write a test that produces an identity signature over digest_of(payload) through the other protocol's signing path and confirm VerifiedRecord::verify accepts a record binding it to a foreign endpoint key.

scanner_findings.title: Record signatures do not bind a network identifier, so a record signed for one network verifies in any network
scanner_findings.prerequisites: Two networks (closed and open, or two closed networks) use the same identity and endpoint keys and the same record format. A record signed for network A is then offered to network B. The membership certificate, which is what ties a record to a closed network, is outside the signed bytes and can be stripped (a known limit).
scanner_findings.impact: Records are not separated by network in the signed content. The record check relies on the membership check alone to scope records to a network, so a record signed for one network is valid cryptographically in any network that accepts records without a certificate. Impact depends on how networks are deployed, which the supplied source does not show.
scanner_findings.evidence: pub const RECORD_DOMAIN: &[u8] = b"golem-p2p/node-record/v1\0"; the digest is SHA-256 over RECORD_DOMAIN and the payload only, and the payload (NodeRecord) has no network or chain field.
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Add a network identifier (for example a hash of the network name or the membership root key) to the signed payload or to the domain tag, and check it on verification.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Confirm whether any deployment accepts records from more than one network with the same keys. Test a record signed in one network verifying under another network's policy.

scanner_findings.title: A valid signature has two accepted byte encodings (v of 0/1 and 27/28), so one record can exist as two different byte strings
scanner_findings.prerequisites: An attacker holds a valid record and can rewrite the v byte of an identity signature from 0 to 27 or 28 to 1 (or the reverse). No key is needed.
scanner_findings.impact: The same signed content gets a second valid encoding. The store compares records by raw bytes (VerifiedRecord equality and compare in store.rs), so the rewritten copy with the same seq is treated as Older and is not stored as Same. The duplicate can take up store and directory space and makes byte-level dedup and caching unreliable. No signature is forged and no content changes.
scanner_findings.evidence: v @ (0 | 1) => v, v @ (27 | 28) => v - 27, and in store.rs compare(): Some(e) if e.seq() == rec.seq() && e == rec => Slot::Same, with equality defined as self.inner.bytes == other.inner.bytes.
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Accept only one v form for recovery (0/1, since the module documents yagna's raw format), or normalize v before storing and compare records by a canonical digest of the payload plus signatures.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Write a test that rewrites v from 0 to 27 on a valid record and checks that VerifiedRecord::verify accepts it and the store treats it as a separate, non-Same record.

scanner_findings.title: Pruner task leaks when serve_with_policy future is dropped
scanner_findings.prerequisites: The caller drops the future returned by serve or serve_with_policy, which the doc comment at line 56 says is how the server is stopped. This is an ordinary runtime condition, not remote input.
scanner_findings.impact: The abort at line 84 runs only after axum::serve returns normally. If the future is dropped mid-serve, the spawned pruner keeps running forever, holding an Arc to the store and calling prune every minute. A process that starts and stops the directory repeatedly accumulates such tasks.
scanner_findings.evidence: let pruner = { let store = store.clone(); tokio::spawn(async move { let mut tick = tokio::time::interval(Duration::from_secs(60)); loop { tick.tick().await; store.prune(); } }) }; let res = axum::serve(listener, router_with_policy(store, policy)).await; pruner.abort(); res
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Wrap the JoinHandle in a guard struct whose Drop impl calls abort, or run the pruner inside the same future with tokio::select! so it is cancelled with the server.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Demonstrated code defect by reading. Confirm with a test that drops the serve future and checks that the pruner task is finished or that the store's Arc strong count returns to 1.

scanner_findings.title: Record verification runs CPU-bound signature recovery on the async runtime
scanner_findings.prerequisites: An anonymous client sends many PUT requests, each a maximum-size record with up to 16 identities and one endpoint signature, which is about 17 signature checks per request (see the known limit on signature cost).
scanner_findings.impact: VerifiedRecord::verify is synchronous and runs directly in the axum handler without spawn_blocking. Enough concurrent PUTs could occupy all tokio worker threads and delay other tasks, including the pruner and health checks. This is hypothesis-level: the per-request cost has not been measured here, and the known limit already covers flood cost.
scanner_findings.evidence: async fn put_record(State(dir): State<Dir>, body: Bytes) -> Response { let rec = match VerifiedRecord::verify(&body) { Ok(rec) => rec, ...
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Run verification with tokio::task::spawn_blocking, or bound concurrent verifications with a semaphore, and measure per-PUT latency under load.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Benchmark PUT throughput with 16-identity records and check whether health latency rises under concurrent load on a small worker pool.

scanner_findings.title: Records accept and the public directory serves internal and container bridge addresses to anyone
scanner_findings.prerequisites: Any node that signs its own record, or any client that sends a record it signed with its own identity and endpoint keys, can list arbitrary direct_addrs such as 172.17.0.1 or other private addresses. The directory accepts such records with no address filtering, and GET /v1/records/{node_id} returns them to any anonymous HTTP client.
scanner_findings.impact: Host network details (Docker bridge subnets, LAN addresses) are published to every party that can query the directory and to every peer that dials the record. This is the internal-address disclosure the lens targets. Nothing in validate() or verify_at() rejects private, loopback or link-local addresses, and the in-file test record_with_docker_addrs_verifies asserts that such records are accepted and that peers dial them.
scanner_findings.evidence: pub direct_addrs: Vec<SocketAddr>, with validate() checking only the count (if self.direct_addrs.len() > MAX_DIRECT_ADDRS). The test comment states: Leaving out container bridge addresses is publishing policy, not a verification rule ... still verifies, and peers dial every listed address. directory.rs get_record returns rec.to_bytes() unfiltered.
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Decide the publishing policy in the node, not only by convention. Filter private, loopback, link-local and bridge addresses when signing (sign_record_with_membership), and have the directory refuse or strip them on PUT. Keep the test, but assert the filtered result rather than acceptance.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Demonstrated in source, not run: PUT a record signed with a 172.17.0.1 direct address to a running directory, then GET it anonymously. Confirm the address is returned. Also confirm how the membership check (not in the supplied source) treats these addresses.

scanner_findings.title: Verification error text is echoed verbatim to unauthenticated HTTP clients
scanner_findings.prerequisites: An anonymous client sends a PUT /v1/records request with arbitrary bytes. Any reachable directory answers with the text of the RecordError.
scanner_findings.impact: The remote party learns which validation step failed, including the identity that failed to sign, the relay-URL and identity-count rules, and the membership policy message on line 96. This is more detail than a rejected publisher needs, and it helps an attacker tune forged records. It does not leak secret keys, and the response is only as verbose as the Display strings in record.rs and the membership module.
scanner_findings.evidence: Err(e) => return (StatusCode::BAD_REQUEST, e.to_string()).into_response(), and on line 96 (StatusCode::FORBIDDEN, e.to_string()). RecordError::IdentitySignature(NodeId) is declared as #[error("identity {0} did not sign this record")], so the response names a specific identity.
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Return a fixed, generic message such as invalid record (400) and a generic forbidden message (403), and log the detailed RecordError server-side with the peer address and a rate limit. Do not log untrusted record content without escaping.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Hypothesis on the wording's severity. The membership policy's error text is not in the supplied source, so its content is unknown and needs review in membership.rs.

scanner_findings.title: Library API exports raw identity secret keys with no restriction or zeroization
scanner_findings.prerequisites: A caller of the public InMemorySigner API calls secret(id). Nothing reachable from the network calls it, so an attacker needs code-level access to the process or to a caller that exposes the value.
scanner_findings.impact: The function returns the 32-byte secp256k1 secret of an identity as a plain copied array with no zeroization, no restriction and no doc(hidden). The module's stated design is that this crate never needs a secret key. Any logging, serialization or debug dump of the returned value would leak an identity key, and the returned copies are not wiped from memory.
scanner_findings.evidence: pub fn secret(&self, id: NodeId) -> Option<[u8; 32]> { let keys = self.keys.lock().expect("poisoned"); keys.get(&id).map(|e| e.key.to_bytes().into()) } with the doc comment: Returns the raw secret key of an identity, for persisting test keys.
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Gate the method behind #[cfg(test)] or a test-only feature, or mark it #[doc(hidden)] and return a wrapper type with a redacted Debug and zeroize-on-drop. Confirm no production path uses it.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Check the call sites in the CLI and other crates (not supplied) for any production use that writes the key to a file, log or command line.

scanner_findings.title: Connection table can be filled by cheap valid handshakes that then idle indefinitely
scanner_findings.prerequisites: An anonymous peer that can generate valid records for its own endpoint key (records cost nothing, per the known limits). It opens QUIC connections, completes a Hello with a valid record, and then keeps each connection alive without sending application traffic (for example by QUIC keep-alives or an open idle control stream).
scanner_findings.impact: The only limit on established connections is the global max_connections check, which defaults to 1024. Once that many idle connections are registered, every honest inbound handshake is refused with incoming.refuse(). The control_reader read has no timeout, so nothing closes a connection that only stays silent. This is a denial of service against all inbound peers from one attacker process, with no per-source or per-identity bound.
scanner_findings.evidence: Check: 'if open >= self.config.max_connections { incoming.refuse(); return false; }' (line 1100). Registration: 'conns.insert(c.stable_id(), c.clone());' (register, ~line 1252). Read with no timeout: 'm = wire::read_frame::<Control>(&mut recv, MAX_CONTROL_FRAME) => m,' (control_reader, line 1658). The handshake timeout applies only before Welcome.
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Add a per-source-address or per-identity cap on established connections, and reserve some capacity for dialers that are already known. Close connections that have sent no control or application traffic for a bounded time. Test: open max_connections valid handshakes from one process with keep-alives and check whether a new honest dial is refused.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Hypothesis. Needs a test: fill the table from one process with valid Hellos and keep-alives, then confirm an honest peer is refused. Also check the iroh/quinn default idle timeout and keep-alive, which are not in the supplied source.

scanner_findings.title: Application stream header tasks are bounded only per connection, so the total is connections times 256
scanner_findings.prerequisites: Up to 1024 established connections (see the previous finding), each opening the maximum of 256 concurrent bidirectional streams and sending no header bytes.
scanner_findings.impact: Every accepted stream spawns a task that waits up to handshake_timeout (10 s) for the KIND_APP byte and header, before any identity check. With 1024 connections, about 262,000 tasks and their QUIC stream state can be live at once. A reset frees a slot, so the attacker can keep reopening streams. Memory and scheduler load grow with the total, and nothing caps it globally.
scanner_findings.evidence: stream_acceptor: 'let Ok((send, recv)) = res else { break };' followed by 'tokio::spawn(handle_app_stream(inner.clone(), c.clone(), send, recv));' (line 1724). handle_app_stream waits on 'tokio::time::timeout(inner.config.handshake_timeout, async { if wire::read_kind(&mut recv).await? != KIND_APP ...' (lines 1734-1735). max_concurrent_bidi_streams is VarInt::from_u32(256) (line 491), which is per connection.
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Put a global semaphore on pending header reads, with a short header deadline, and count pending headers per connection. Refuse or reset when the cap is reached, before spawning the task. Test: 1024 connections x 256 idle streams, then measure task count and memory.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Hypothesis. Needs a load test that measures spawned tasks and RSS with many idle streams on many connections.

scanner_findings.title: Record updates from each connection cost full signature verification, paced per connection only
scanner_findings.prerequisites: An established connection (obtainable cheaply, see the first finding). The peer sends well-formed Update frames, each a fresh record signed by its own keys with a higher seq than before, or stale ones, at the pacing rate.
scanner_findings.impact: Every Update is fully verified (up to 17 signatures for a record with 16 identities plus the endpoint key) before the seq check. Pacing is 100 ms per connection, so about 10 verifications per second per connection. The pacing does not limit the total across connections. With 1024 connections the aggregate is about 10,000 record verifications per second, roughly 170,000 signature checks per second, which is a CPU denial of service. The comment says QUIC flow control provides backpressure, but flow control does not limit verification cost per frame.
scanner_findings.evidence: 'let new = match VerifiedRecord::verify(&record) {' (line 1675), after 'next_allowed = tokio::time::Instant::now() + UPDATE_INTERVAL;' (line 1660) and before 'if new.seq() <= current.seq() { continue; }' (line 1698). Constant: 'const UPDATE_INTERVAL: Duration = Duration::from_millis(100);' (line 631).
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Check the cheap fields first (endpoint ID, instance ID, seq greater than current, expires_at) before verifying the signatures. Add a global verification budget across connections, or a per-connection budget that closes the connection after repeated stale or duplicate updates. Test: one connection that sends stale valid updates at the maximum rate, then multiply by the connection count.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Hypothesis. Needs a benchmark of verify cost and a test that counts verifications per second with many connections. Whether checking seq before verifying is safe depends on record.rs, which is not supplied.

scanner_findings.title: Every incoming QUIC connection spawns a task before the handshake limit is checked
scanner_findings.prerequisites: A flood of incoming QUIC initial packets that iroh surfaces through accept(), while the 128 handshake permits are in use.
scanner_findings.impact: accept_loop spawns a task for each incoming connection without any bound. Only then does accept_incoming acquire a permit or refuse. Under a flood the task count grows with the arrival rate until tasks finish. The refuse path is cheap, so this is mainly a scheduling and memory cost, and its size depends on how iroh bounds its own accept queue, which is not in the supplied source.
scanner_findings.evidence: accept_loop: 'let Some(incoming) = incoming else { break };' then 'tokio::spawn(inner.clone().handle_incoming(incoming));' (lines 1408-1409). accept_incoming: 'let Ok(_permit) = self.handshakes.clone().try_acquire_owned() else { incoming.refuse(); return false; };' (lines 1096-1099).
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Try to take the handshake permit in accept_loop before spawning, and refuse inline when none is free. Test: flood incoming connections while the 128 permits are held and watch the task count.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Hypothesis. Needs a test that counts live tasks under an incoming flood, plus the iroh accept queue limit from its source.

scanner_findings.title: Expired peer certificates stay usable while the membership sweep is stalled, and stream/connection reuse never re-checks membership
scanner_findings.prerequisites: Closed network with a membership policy. A member peer's certificate reaches expiry while our node still holds an open connection to it. The registry call in the renewal branch of membership_loop stalls (the issuer call has no timeout in this file), so the loop never reaches its 5 s sweep tick. Alternatively, the attacker is a member whose certificate expired and who keeps the connection open after the sweep has been starved.
scanner_findings.impact: Expiry of a peer's membership is enforced only by the sweep in membership_loop (lines 1517-1530). While that loop is blocked in the renewal branch, which awaits the registry at line 1536 with no timeout in this file, expired peers stay in the connection table. Connection::open_bi (line 2191), find_connection (lines 912-935) and handle_app_stream (lines 1751-1765) check only the record's identities, never check_member, so an expired or revoked member can keep opening and receiving application streams until the sweep runs. The lookup in find_connection also returns such connections to callers of connect and request.
scanner_findings.evidence: membership_loop: "_ = sweep.tick() => { ... if let Err(e) = inner.check_member(&peer) { ... c.inner.conn.close(codes::NOT_MEMBER, b"membership expired"); } }" and in the same select: "_ = tokio::time::sleep_until(due) => { ... let res = certify(&m, ...).await; ...". handle_app_stream: "let peer = c.peer(); let code = if !inner.local_record().contains(&header.to) {...} else if !peer.contains(&header.from) { Some(codes::SENDER_NOT_BOUND) }" with no membership check.
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Run the expiry sweep in its own task, or give the renewal future a timeout and run it outside the sweep's select. Also add a cheap check in handle_app_stream and in find_connection/Connection::open_bi that the peer's certificate is still valid at the moment of use (check_member on c.peer()), and close the connection on failure.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Hypothesis, not a demonstrated defect. Write a test with a mock issuer that blocks certify and a short-lived peer certificate: after the peer's certificate expires and the issuer call hangs, check whether an application stream from that peer is still accepted and whether connect() still returns the old connection. The issuer implementation is not in the supplied files, so whether it has its own timeout is unknown.

scanner_findings.title: Identity claims on an open connection are not re-checked against record expiry
scanner_findings.prerequisites: A peer endpoint E holds a valid record R that lists identity X and expires at time T. E keeps its QUIC connection open past T and sends no newer record. The record's identity owner stops re-signing for E, so R is never renewed. This is a hypothesis: whether the expiry bound is meant to revoke authority on live connections is not documented in the supplied files.
scanner_findings.impact: After R expires, handle_app_stream still accepts streams whose from is X on that connection, and find_connection still routes requests for X to it. The signature that authorised X on E is no longer valid under the record's own expiry rule, but nothing re-checks it on the live connection. Only membership expiry is swept (membership_loop), not record expiry.
scanner_findings.evidence: handle_app_stream: "} else if !peer.contains(&header.from) {" where peer = c.peer(). register stores the verified record and never reads expires_at: "let (peer_tx, peer_rx) = watch::channel(peer.clone());". membership_loop sweeps only check_member(&peer), and find_connection filters only on is_closed, contains, seq and is_superseded. control_reader accepts an update only when VerifiedRecord::verify succeeds and new.seq() > current.seq().
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Keep the record's expires_at with the connection (for example in ConnInner, or read it from peer.expires_at()). Check it in find_connection and in handle_app_stream, and have membership_loop, or a similar sweep, close connections whose peer record has expired, with a dedicated close code. Add a test that a connection whose peer record has expired stops accepting streams claiming that peer's identities.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Confirm in record.rs that expires_at is exposed and that VerifiedRecord::verify does not re-check expiry at use time. Then write a test: establish a connection with a short-lived record, advance time past expiry without a new update, and check that open_bi and handle_app_stream still accept identity X.

scanner_findings.title: Connection cap is checked against a snapshot taken before the handshake, so concurrent handshakes can overshoot max_connections
scanner_findings.prerequisites: A remote peer opens many QUIC connections at once. Up to 128 handshakes (MAX_PENDING_HANDSHAKES) can run in parallel, and each handle_incoming task runs accept_incoming independently.
scanner_findings.impact: Each handshake reads conns.len() at line 1095 and compares it at line 1100, but registration happens only after several awaits (lines 1104-1204). Many handshakes can pass the check together, so the number of registered connections can exceed config.max_connections (default 1024) by up to about 127. This is a demonstrated code defect in the check-then-act ordering, though the overshoot is bounded.
scanner_findings.evidence: let open = self.conns.lock().expect("poisoned").len(); ... if open >= self.config.max_connections { incoming.refuse(); return false; } ... self.register(conn, peer, send, recv, local_rx, Direction::Incoming);
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Reserve a slot atomically before the handshake, for example with a second semaphore sized max_connections acquired with try_acquire_owned and moved into the registered Connection. Alternatively re-check the count under the conns lock inside register and close the connection if the cap is already reached.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: A test that opens about 200 concurrent incoming handshakes against max_connections of 10 and counts the registered connections. The demonstrated part is the ordering; the size of the overshoot depends on scheduling.

scanner_findings.title: request_timeout of Duration::MAX (or any huge value) panics on Instant overflow in open_bi
scanner_findings.prerequisites: The application sets Builder::request_timeout to a very large Duration, such as Duration::MAX as a way of saying no timeout. The panic is local and needs no remote input.
scanner_findings.impact: Adding a huge Duration to tokio::time::Instant::now() panics with an overflow. The panic happens in request_from or open_bi, in the caller's task, before any stream is opened.
scanner_findings.evidence: let deadline = timeout.map(|t| tokio::time::Instant::now() + t);  (request_timeout is stored unchecked by Builder::request_timeout at line 365-366: self.config.request_timeout = t;)
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Validate the configured timeout in Builder::request_timeout, clamping it to a sane maximum, or compute the deadline with checked_add and treat overflow as no deadline.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: A unit test that sets request_timeout(Duration::MAX) and calls request on a connected pair. This is a demonstrated panic on a documented-style input, but it is reachable only through local configuration.

scanner_findings.title: Sequence number computation adds 1 to min_seq without a checked addition, so min_seq of u64::MAX overflows
scanner_findings.prerequisites: The application calls Builder::min_seq with u64::MAX or another value near the limit, for example from a persisted sequence number that was corrupted. The same expression also appears in certify at line 760.
scanner_findings.impact: In debug builds, prev_seq + 1 panics during bind, which makes startup fail. In release builds it wraps to 0, and the max with the clock value hides the wrap. Either way the strictly increasing sequence property the comment promises is lost. Not remotely reachable.
scanner_findings.evidence: let seq = (prev_seq + 1).max(now.as_micros() as u64);  (bind passes self.min_seq as prev_seq at line 466 and 553)
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Use prev_seq.saturating_add(1) in both places, so the clock value takes over at the limit, and document min_seq as capped.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: A debug-build test with min_seq(u64::MAX) that calls bind. Hypothesis about the caller's persisted values, which are outside this source.

scanner_findings.title: Peer-controlled QUIC close reason is turned into a String in the Disconnected event
scanner_findings.prerequisites: A connected peer closes the connection with an application close reason containing arbitrary bytes, such as newlines or terminal escape sequences. An application subscribes to Event::Disconnected and writes its reason field to logs or a terminal without escaping.
scanner_findings.impact: Forged log lines or terminal escape sequences could be injected by a remote peer, if the consuming application logs the reason unescaped. Nothing in this file writes the reason to logs itself.
scanner_findings.evidence: close_watcher: let reason = c.inner.conn.closed().await; ... inner.emit(Event::Disconnected { peer: c.peer(), reason: reason.to_string(), });
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Document that Event::Disconnected.reason is untrusted peer text, or replace it with a sanitized form (for example the QUIC error code and a length-limited printable subset) before emitting the event.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Hypothesis. Confirm what quinn's Display of ApplicationClosed prints for peer-supplied reason bytes, and write a test that closes with a newline-containing reason and checks the event string.

scanner_findings.title: Private and VPN direct addresses are sent to every authenticated peer inside the record
scanner_findings.prerequisites: An attacker completes the handshake as an ordinary peer in an open network, which needs no membership. The node's LAN, VPN or non-default interface addresses are present in its published direct addresses, which the default policy only partly filters (it removes container bridges, and VPN interfaces are published by default).
scanner_findings.impact: A remote peer learns internal address layout (RFC1918 LAN addresses and VPN addresses) that it does not need for connectivity, since those addresses are also sent in Welcome and Update frames to every authenticated peer.
scanner_findings.evidence: build_and_sign: let record = NodeRecord { ... relay_urls, direct_addrs, }; and accept_incoming sends Control::Welcome { record: local.to_bytes().to_vec() } (line 1195) with the same record.
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Limit the record sent over the wire to the addresses needed for dialing, or keep private addresses out of the record unless the user opts in. Document that the default publishes private addresses to peers.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Design question more than a code defect. Confirm with the design document whether publishing private addresses to every peer is intended, and check the addrs::select output for a typical host.

scanner_findings.title: Node registrations are unbounded and each one rewrites the whole state file
scanner_findings.prerequisites: An account token holder (any account; accounts are created by the admin) sends PUT /v1/nodes/{id} in a loop with fresh 20-byte node IDs.
scanner_findings.impact: Nothing caps the number of registered nodes per account or in total, so the state map and the state file grow without bound. Each mutation clones the entire state (line 362) and serializes and fsyncs the whole JSON file (lines 176 and 364), so per-request cost and disk writes grow with the total registered count, and the registry slows down and can run out of disk.
scanner_findings.evidence: In add_node: "_ => { st.nodes.insert(id.to_string(), account.clone()); Ok(account) }" and in mutate: "let before = st.clone(); let out = f(&mut st)?; if let Err(e) = st.save(&s.path)". save() does serde_json::to_string_pretty(self) and write_private(...) with sync_all().
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Add a configurable maximum number of nodes per account and in total, refuse with 429 or 507 above it, and consider a per-account quota. Persist incrementally (append-only log or a database) instead of rewriting the full JSON on every change, and avoid cloning the full state for rollback (apply the change to a copy of the single entry, or undo it).
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Demonstrated code defect for the missing cap and the full-state clone and rewrite per call. Measuring how far the latency grows with N (for example 10^5 to 10^6 nodes) needs a test with the registry server.

scanner_findings.title: State mutex is held across blocking file writes and fsync inside async handlers
scanner_findings.prerequisites: Any valid account or admin token holder sends many PUT or DELETE requests to /v1/nodes or /v1/accounts.
scanner_findings.impact: mutate() takes a std::sync::Mutex and then calls synchronous file I/O with sync_all, inside an async axum handler. That blocks a tokio worker thread for the duration of each save, and every other handler, including /v1/certify, which needs the same lock, waits behind it. Sustained writes can starve the runtime and delay certificate issuance for honest nodes.
scanner_findings.evidence: fn mutate<T>(s: &Shared, f: ...) { let mut st = s.state.lock().expect("poisoned"); let before = st.clone(); let out = f(&mut st)?; if let Err(e) = st.save(&s.path) { ... } } and in the handlers: async fn add_node(...) calls mutate(&s, ...) directly. The save path ends in std::fs::File sync_all via write_private.
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Run the save on a blocking thread (tokio::task::spawn_blocking) or move persistence to a background writer, and keep the critical section short. Also replace expect("poisoned") with error handling so a panic in one handler does not turn into a panic for every later request.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Code-level blocking is visible in the source. The size of the throughput drop depends on the disk and needs a benchmark with concurrent PUTs and certify requests.

scanner_findings.title: Certify endpoint does signature work for every anonymous request with no rate limit
scanner_findings.prerequisites: Any unauthenticated client on the network that can reach the registry, behind the TLS proxy, sends many POST /v1/certify requests with valid or near-valid records of up to MAX_RECORD_SIZE bytes.
scanner_findings.impact: Each request runs VerifiedRecord::verify (up to 17 signature checks, per the record limits) before any cheap check, and then, if the identities are registered, signs a new certificate. Nothing in the server bounds this rate, so an anonymous sender can use CPU in proportion to request rate. The directory has the same cost, and its documentation places rate limits in the proxy, but this registry's docs do not say so.
scanner_findings.evidence: async fn certify(State(s): State<Arc<Shared>>, body: Bytes) -> Response { let proof = match VerifiedRecord::verify(&body) { ... }; let st = s.state.lock()...; match st.certify(&proof) { Ok(cert) => ... MembershipCert::issue(...) } }. Only DefaultBodyLimit::max(MAX_RECORD_SIZE) bounds the input.
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Check the cheap things first (network name, identity count, and whether each identity is registered, which needs no signature check, although the record must be verified before its identities can be trusted, so the ordering may need to stay). Add a concurrency or per-source rate limit on /v1/certify, or document that the proxy must provide one, and consider caching certificates for an unchanged (endpoint, identities, sequence) tuple.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Hypothesis. Needs a load test to measure the CPU cost per request on the target hardware and to confirm no rate limit exists in the deployment proxy, which is outside the supplied source.

scanner_findings.title: Registry server sets no connection, header or body-read timeouts and no concurrency cap
scanner_findings.prerequisites: A remote client that can open TCP connections to the registry listen address (or to the proxy that forwards to it) and then sends headers or bodies very slowly or not at all.
scanner_findings.impact: serve_with calls axum::serve with no read timeout, no concurrency limit and no connection cap. Slow or idle connections can hold file descriptors and tasks for an unbounded time. The body size is bounded by DefaultBodyLimit, but the time to send it is not.
scanner_findings.evidence: pub async fn serve_with(...) -> std::io::Result<()> { let app = router_with(path, options)...; axum::serve(listener, app).await } and the router only sets .layer(DefaultBodyLimit::max(MAX_RECORD_SIZE)).
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Put a tower timeout layer (for example TimeoutLayer or ConcurrencyLimitLayer) on the router, or set hyper header and read timeouts through a custom accept loop, and document that the proxy must enforce them if the server does not.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Hypothesis. Needs a slowloris-style test against the built server, and a check of which timeouts the axum and hyper versions in Cargo.lock already apply by default.

scanner_findings.title: Registry client sends bearer tokens over plain HTTP without a scheme check
scanner_findings.prerequisites: An operator or script points the CLI or RegistryClient at an http:// registry URL (the registry serves plain HTTP by design), and an on-path observer can read the traffic between the client and the registry.
scanner_findings.impact: The admin token or an account token is sent in cleartext in the Authorization header. An observer can then create accounts, register or remove nodes, or list all nodes. Nothing in the client rejects http:// bases, and with_tls accepts any URL.
scanner_findings.evidence: RegistryClient::with_tls(base, tls) builds the client without checking base.scheme(); call() does: if let Some(t) = token { req = req.bearer_auth(t); }
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Reject non-https base URLs in RegistryClient::with_tls and new unless an explicit insecure opt-in is set, or at least warn when a token is sent to an http URL.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Test that RegistryClient::new(http://...) followed by call(GET, v1/nodes, Some(token)) sends the token in cleartext. Confirm whether the CLI documents https as required.

scanner_findings.title: Existing temporary state file keeps its old permissions, so the signing key can be written to a more readable file
scanner_findings.prerequisites: A local user can create or leave behind the fixed name state.tmp (path with_extension tmp) before the registry saves, with permissions wider than 0600 (for example a leftover file from an earlier crash or a file created under a permissive umask).
scanner_findings.impact: OpenOptions::mode(0o600) applies only when the file is created. On an existing file, truncate keeps its mode, so the state file, which holds the registry signing key and the admin hash, is written into a file that other local users may read. The rename then moves that file into place as the state file.
scanner_findings.evidence: let tmp = path.with_extension("tmp"); ... write_private(&tmp, text.as_bytes()) ... fn write_private: .truncate(true).mode(0o600).open(path)?; with no fchmod or check of an existing file's mode.
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Write to a unique temporary name created with create_new(true), or call set_permissions(0o600) on the opened file before writing, and fsync the parent directory after the rename.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Test: pre-create state.tmp with mode 0644, run a save, and check the resulting state file mode. Depends on whether the state directory is shared with untrusted local users.

scanner_findings.title: Certificate signature check accepts malleable ed25519 signatures, so one certificate has many encodings
scanner_findings.prerequisites: An attacker holds any valid certificate issued by the registry, which a node can obtain legitimately for itself, and can re-encode the signature bytes.
scanner_findings.impact: PublicKey::verify does not enforce a canonical signature encoding, so a different byte string for the same certificate also verifies. The comment says one certificate has one encoding, and that property is false. Anything that deduplicates or keys by certificate bytes, such as a revocation list or a cache of seen certificates, could be bypassed. No authorization decision here changes, since the payload is still signed by the trusted key.
scanner_findings.evidence: issuer.verify(&digest(&wire.payload), &iroh::Signature::from_bytes(&sig)).map_err(|_| MembershipError::Signature)?; and the comment 'one certificate, one encoding' at decode.
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Reject signatures with a non-canonical S value (s must be below the group order) or use verify_strict if available, and keep the one-encoding claim only if that is enforced. Check whether any caller keys on certificate bytes.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Test that a signature with S replaced by S + L verifies. Check the callers outside the supplied files before rating it higher.

scanner_findings.title: Registry state temp file keeps pre-existing permissions and follows symlinks, so the signing key can be written to a world-readable or attacker-chosen file
scanner_findings.prerequisites: An attacker can create or replace the file registry.tmp (path.with_extension("tmp")) in the state directory before a save, for example a leftover file with mode 0644 or a symlink. This needs local write access to the state directory, which is already close to owning the registry.
scanner_findings.impact: Each save writes the full state JSON, including the hex Ed25519 secret key that signs all membership certificates, into registry.tmp. write_private uses OpenOptions::mode(0o600), but mode only applies when the file is created. If the file already exists, its old mode is kept, so the signing key can be readable by other users. Without O_NOFOLLOW or create_new, a symlink at that path redirects the key write to an arbitrary file. A leaked signing key lets the attacker issue certificates for any endpoint and identity in the network.
scanner_findings.evidence: Line 175: let tmp = path.with_extension("tmp"); line 177: write_private(&tmp, text.as_bytes()); lines 240-245: OpenOptions::new().write(true).create(true).truncate(true).mode(0o600).open(path)?; The state struct holds secret_key: String, documented as 'The signing key, hex.'
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Create the temporary file with create_new(true) and a random suffix in the same directory (for example via the tempfile crate), so an existing file or symlink is never reused. Set permissions with set_permissions(0o600) on the open handle before writing, or use fchmod. Then rename into place. Optionally refuse to load a state file whose mode allows group or other access.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Hypothesis, not run: create registry.tmp with mode 0644 (or as a symlink to a file in another directory), call RegistryState::save, and check the resulting file mode and target. A unit test in the registry module would show it.

scanner_findings.title: Registry holds a std Mutex across blocking file I/O and a full state clone in async handlers
scanner_findings.prerequisites: Any account holder (or the admin) issues PUT or DELETE on /v1/nodes or account changes while the state file lives on slow storage. No attacker-controlled panic is needed.
scanner_findings.impact: mutate() takes the std Mutex, clones the whole RegistryState, then calls st.save(), which does a synchronous write, sync_all and rename on a tokio worker thread while the guard is held. Every concurrent /v1/certify, /v1/info and listing handler blocks on the same lock, so one slow fsync stalls certification for all nodes and ties up runtime threads. The clone is also O(total state) per mutation. This is a demonstrated code pattern; the size of the stall is a hypothesis that needs a load or slow-disk test.
scanner_findings.evidence: let mut st = s.state.lock().expect("poisoned"); let before = st.clone(); let out = f(&mut st)?; if let Err(e) = st.save(&s.path) { *st = before; ... } (save at line 174 calls write_private(...) and f.sync_all())
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Mutate a clone or a small journal outside the lock, or use tokio::sync::Mutex with spawn_blocking around the file write, so the lock is never held across blocking I/O. Replace expect("poisoned") with explicit handling so one panic does not turn into permanent 500s on every later request.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Benchmark /v1/certify latency while PUT /v1/nodes runs against a state file on a throttled disk; confirm the stall and the runtime worker occupancy.

scanner_findings.title: certify computes now + cert_lifetime_s unchecked, under the lock, so a bad state-file value poisons the registry
scanner_findings.prerequisites: An operator or someone with write access to the 0600 state file sets cert_lifetime_s close to u64::MAX. RegistryState::load only validates the signing key, not the lifetime, and init's 60 s to 7 day bounds do not apply on load.
scanner_findings.impact: now + self.cert_lifetime_s overflows: a panic in debug builds, a wrapped expiry in release. The panic happens inside the certify handler while s.state's guard is held, so the Mutex is poisoned. Every later handler then panics on expect("poisoned") at lines 361, 373, 392, 469 and 542, a permanent registry outage until restart. Remote input does not reach this value directly. A lifetime above MAX_CERT_LIFETIME is also issued without any check, which peers would refuse.
scanner_findings.evidence: expires_at: now + self.cert_lifetime_s, inside certify(); load() only calls st.key()?; handlers use s.state.lock().expect("poisoned")
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Validate cert_lifetime_s in load() against the same bounds as init (60 s to MAX_CERT_LIFETIME), use checked_add in certify, and return an error instead of panicking under the lock.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Unit test: load a state file with cert_lifetime_s = u64::MAX and call certify; expect a clean error, not a panic or poisoned lock.

scanner_findings.title: CLI account add creates the account on the registry before checking that the token file can be written
scanner_findings.prerequisites: The operator runs registry account add with a --token-out path that appears between the exists() check and the write (a race), or the path is unwritable. write_secret is not in the supplied source, so its create-new behaviour is unknown.
scanner_findings.impact: The POST at line 217 creates the account and returns its only copy of the token. If write_secret then fails, the token is lost, the account name is permanently taken (a later add gets 409), and the operator cannot recover without an admin account removal. This is a check-then-use ordering problem, not a remote one.
scanner_findings.evidence: if token_out.exists() { bail!(...) } let token = call(&c, "POST", &format!("v1/accounts/{name}"), Some(&admin)).await?; write_secret(&token_out, &format!("{}\n", token.trim()))?;
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Write the token file with create_new before the remote call, or write to a temporary file and rename after success, so a local failure happens before the account exists.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Confirm write_secret's behaviour in crates/golem-p2p-cli/src/main.rs; test with an unwritable --token-out directory and check whether the account exists afterwards.

scanner_findings.title: Unescaped text from a registry or proxy answer is printed to the operator's terminal
scanner_findings.prerequisites: The operator uses the CLI against a registry URL that returns attacker-chosen text. This happens if the registry or a proxy in front of it is compromised, or if the URL is plain http and an on-path attacker can rewrite the answer (see the cleartext finding).
scanner_findings.impact: error_text keeps the first line of the body (up to 200 chars, any control characters included) and returns it as the error message. The CLI prints it through bail!, and list commands print the raw body with print!. A remote party can therefore put ANSI escape sequences or forged text into the admin's terminal.
scanner_findings.evidence: let line: String = body.lines().next().unwrap_or("").chars().take(200).collect(); ... format!("HTTP {status}: {line}") ; CLI: print!("{}", call(&c, "GET", "v1/accounts", Some(&admin)).await?)
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Replace control characters (including ESC and other C0/C1 controls) with escapes or spaces before building the message, and sanitize the raw body in the CLI list commands as well. Add a test that a body containing \x1b[ is rendered without the control byte.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Demonstrated code defect by reading. A unit test with a body containing an ANSI escape would confirm that the control byte reaches the error string unchanged.

scanner_findings.title: Account and admin bearer tokens are sent to any URL scheme, including plain http, with the default redirect policy
scanner_findings.prerequisites: An operator sets the registry URL to an http:// address (the registry itself serves plain HTTP by design), or the registry answers with a redirect. An on-path attacker can then read the token or send the client elsewhere.
scanner_findings.impact: RegistryClient::call attaches the bearer token with no check that the scheme is https. The client is built with reqwest defaults, which follow redirects, so the token may be carried to other hosts depending on the reqwest version. A leaked admin token gives control of all accounts; a leaked account token allows registering or removing nodes.
scanner_findings.evidence: if let Some(t) = token { req = req.bearer_auth(t); } ... let mut req = self.client.request(method, url);  (client built with .timeout and .connect_timeout only; no redirect policy set)
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Reject non-https registry URLs for token-bearing calls unless an explicit insecure flag is given. Set redirect(reqwest::redirect::Policy::none()) for the management client, so tokens are never forwarded.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Hypothesis. A test against a local http server that checks whether the bearer header is sent, and a redirect test to a second host, would confirm the behaviour of the reqwest version in use.

scanner_findings.title: Directory URL with credentials can end up in error messages and warning logs
scanner_findings.prerequisites: The directory base URL contains userinfo (https://user:password@host/), which an operator might configure. A publish failure then logs the error through the warn! in MultiDiscovery::publish.
scanner_findings.impact: self.error includes the full base URL, so any password in it is written to error values and logs. reqwest error text may include the URL too.
scanner_findings.evidence: fn error(&self, e: impl fmt::Display) -> DiscoveryError { DiscoveryError::Service(format!("directory {}: {e}", self.base)) }
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Reject base URLs with a username or password in HttpDirectory::with_tls, or print only the scheme, host and port in error messages.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Hypothesis. Depends on whether reqwest errors include userinfo for the configured base URL. A test that formats the error for a base URL with credentials would confirm it.

scanner_findings.title: Pre-existing temporary state file keeps loose permissions before it is renamed over the state file
scanner_findings.prerequisites: A file with the name of the temporary path (state path with extension tmp) already exists with looser permissions, for example from an earlier run, a copy, or another user who can write to the directory.
scanner_findings.impact: OpenOptions::mode(0o600) applies only when the file is created. write_private truncates an existing file and keeps its permissions. The rename then installs that file as the state file, which holds the registry signing key and admin token hash.
scanner_findings.evidence: let tmp = path.with_extension("tmp"); ... write_private(&tmp, text.as_bytes()) ... std::fs::rename(&tmp, path)  with write_private using .mode(0o600) on open
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Remove the temporary file before creating it, or create it with create_new(true) so that an existing file is an error. Optionally call set_permissions(0o600) on the file before the rename.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Hypothesis. Requires a directory where an attacker or an earlier process left a loose-permission tmp file. A test that pre-creates the tmp file with mode 0644 and checks the state file mode after save would confirm it.

scanner_findings.title: Non-Unix state and token files are written with default permissions
scanner_findings.prerequisites: The registry runs on a non-Unix platform, where the state file contains the signing key and the admin token is written with write_secret.
scanner_findings.impact: The documented mode 0600 is not applied, so the signing key and admin token are written with the default ACL of the directory, which may be readable by other local users.
scanner_findings.evidence: #[cfg(not(unix))] fn write_private(path: &FsPath, data: &[u8]) -> std::io::Result<()> { std::fs::write(path, data) }
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: On Windows, set a restrictive ACL on the file, or refuse to save secrets and document that the state file must be placed in a private directory.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Hypothesis, only relevant if non-Unix deployment is supported. Checking the file ACL after save on Windows would confirm the default permissions.

scanner_findings.title: Download slot released before the stream drains, so lingering downloads escape max_transfers
scanner_findings.prerequisites: A remote peer that can open many QUIC streams on the connection cap and send download requests within max_transfer_size. The peer reads the response slowly or stops reading after write_source has buffered the data.
scanner_findings.impact: The permit is dropped at line 393, before send.stopped() is awaited for up to 10 s at line 399. Each stream that has finished writing still holds quinn send buffers, but no longer counts against max_transfers. Concurrent buffered download streams can therefore exceed the configured limit, bounded only by the connection and stream caps and flow-control windows. This is a demonstrated code ordering in the source; the size of the resulting memory impact needs a test.
scanner_findings.evidence: let permit = try_slot(slots); ... let write = write_source(&mut send, requested, &mut sent); let result = tokio::time::timeout(limits.max_transfer_time, write).await; drop(permit); ... Ok(Ok(())) => { let _ = tokio::time::timeout(Duration::from_secs(10), send.stopped()).await; }
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Hold the permit until after the send.stopped() wait (or until the stream is finished or reset), and bound that wait by the transfer time, not a fixed 10 s, so the slot count covers every stream that still has buffered data.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Write a test with max_transfers 1 and a client that requests a large download and never reads. Open a second download and check whether it is accepted while the first is still in its stopped() wait. Measure the buffered bytes per lingering stream.

scanner_findings.title: Download request phase uses a fresh REQUEST_TIME instead of the request deadline
scanner_findings.prerequisites: A peer sends a download magic and then trickles the byte count slowly, staying just inside the time limit for each read.
scanner_findings.impact: The head read is bounded by deadline (line 129), but the body read at line 145 restarts a new 10 s timer and ignores the deadline. A request can therefore hold a stream for about 20 s before refusal, and about 10 s more if the peer then stops reading at line 399. This doubles the per-stream hold time that REQUEST_TIME is meant to bound. The impact is modest because the stream count is still limited by the connection cap.
scanner_findings.evidence: match tokio::time::timeout(REQUEST_TIME, recv.read_to_end(max)).await { Ok(rest) => req.extend_from_slice(&rest?), Err(_) => req.clear(), }
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Use tokio::time::timeout_at(deadline, ...) at line 145, as the echo path does at line 156, so the whole request phase shares one REQUEST_TIME budget.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Test with a client that sends the source magic and then delays the count digits; measure the time until the server refuses or closes the stream.

scanner_findings.title: Echo reply can be about three times the request size through lossy UTF-8 conversion
scanner_findings.prerequisites: A remote peer sends an echo request of up to MAX_REQUEST bytes consisting of invalid UTF-8 bytes (for example lone 0x80 to 0xFF bytes).
scanner_findings.impact: String::from_utf8_lossy replaces each invalid byte with the three-byte U+FFFD sequence, so a 1 MiB request can produce a reply of about 3 MiB. This is an amplification of about 3x on the largest requests, and each reply is built as a separate formatted String. It is a small, bounded amplification, not an unbounded one.
scanner_findings.evidence: let reply = format!( "{me} to={to} from={from} echo={}", String::from_utf8_lossy(&req) ); inc.respond(reply.as_bytes()).await?;
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Echo the request as raw bytes (or escape non-UTF-8 bytes to a fixed-size form), or reject non-UTF-8 echo requests, so the reply is never larger than the request plus the fixed header.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Send a 1 MiB request of 0x80 bytes and measure the reply length to confirm the expansion factor.

scanner_findings.title: Oversized echo request returns an error without stopping the stream
scanner_findings.prerequisites: A remote peer sends more than MAX_REQUEST - head bytes on an echo stream and then keeps the stream open without finishing it.
scanner_findings.impact: When read_to_end exceeds its limit, the error propagates through rest? at line 157, and the handler returns without calling recv.stop(REFUSED), unlike too_slow. The peer's stream is left open until flow control or connection teardown, with no explicit reset. Memory per stream stays bounded by flow control, so the impact is hypothetical and would need a test to confirm the behaviour of the dropped RecvStream.
scanner_findings.evidence: match tokio::time::timeout_at(deadline, read).await { Ok(rest) => head.extend_from_slice(&rest?), Err(_) => return Err(too_slow(&mut inc)), }
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: On a read_to_end error, call recv.stop(REFUSED) and send.reset(REFUSED) before returning, as too_slow does, so the stream is closed explicitly.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Open an echo stream with MAX_REQUEST + 1 bytes and keep it open without finishing. Check whether the server holds the stream, and whether the peer's send side stays blocked, after the handler returns.

scanner_findings.title: Request-head budget resets: download request read gets a fresh REQUEST_TIME after the shared deadline
scanner_findings.prerequisites: A remote peer opens an application stream and sends the SOURCE_MAGIC prefix, then sends the rest of the request (byte count) slowly or not at all, without finishing the stream.
scanner_findings.impact: The head read is bounded by the shared deadline (line 111, 129), but the source-request read at line 145 uses a new tokio::time::timeout(REQUEST_TIME) that is not tied to that deadline. A stream can therefore be held for up to about 2 x REQUEST_TIME (20 s) before refusal, instead of 10 s. Each such stream occupies a spawned task and a QUIC stream slot, but not a transfer slot. This is a time-bound inconsistency, not a panic; the exposure is bounded by the QUIC stream limits and the connection cap.
scanner_findings.evidence: let deadline = tokio::time::Instant::now() + REQUEST_TIME; ... match tokio::time::timeout_at(deadline, read_head).await { ... } ... match tokio::time::timeout(REQUEST_TIME, recv.read_to_end(max)).await { Ok(rest) => req.extend_from_slice(&rest?), Err(_) => req.clear(), }
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Pass the same deadline into the source-request read: use tokio::time::timeout_at(deadline, recv.read_to_end(max)) so the whole request head shares one REQUEST_TIME budget, as the echo path already does at line 156.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Hypothesis from reading the code: write a test with a peer that sends SOURCE_MAGIC and then stalls, and measure time to refusal before and after the change.

scanner_findings.title: Per-connection handler tasks are detached and never joined or cancelled on shutdown
scanner_findings.prerequisites: The endpoint is closed (ep.accept() returns None) while requests are in flight, for example during CLI shutdown.
scanner_findings.impact: serve() returns as soon as accept() yields None, but the handle() tasks spawned at line 84 are not tracked, so they are neither awaited nor aborted. In-flight transfers can still hold transfer slots and write to the output after the caller has assumed serve is done. Each task is bounded by timeouts (REQUEST_TIME, max_transfer_time, and the 10 s send.stopped wait at line 399), so this is not an indefinite hang. Remote peers cannot exceed the bounds by this path. Whether the process exits before those tasks finish depends on the caller in main.rs, which is not supplied.
scanner_findings.evidence: while let Some(inc) = ep.accept().await { ... tokio::spawn(async move { let from = inc.from(); match handle(inc, &out, &me, &limits, &slots).await { ... } }); }
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Track handlers in a tokio::task::JoinSet and drain or abort it after the accept loop ends, so shutdown order is explicit and output is not written after the caller's shutdown point.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Check the caller in main.rs, which was not supplied, to see whether it waits for serve or exits the process; if it exits, this is a clean-shutdown issue only.

scanner_findings.title: Loopback addresses are published into signed public records
scanner_findings.prerequisites: The node has a loopback interface (lo) carrying 127.0.0.1 or ::1, and it is reported as a direct candidate by iroh. Nothing in HOST_INTERNAL_INTERFACES or the exclude patterns filters lo, so the address passes the filter in select.
scanner_findings.impact: Loopback addresses are signed into the public record and sent to every peer and directory. They are useless to remote peers, since a peer dialing 127.0.0.1 reaches its own host, and they reveal local-only addressing. This runs against the stated goal of keeping internal addresses out of public records. It occupies a slot under the cap, though loopback ranks last.
scanner_findings.evidence: Line 201: `} else if names.iter().all(|n| excluded_iface(n)) {` with excluded_iface only checking is_host_internal or exclude patterns, and the test expectation at line 452: `"127.0.0.1:5",` inside `s.published`. Scope::Loopback ranks last, but nothing removes it.
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Exclude loopback and unspecified addresses (127.0.0.0/8, ::1, 0.0.0.0, ::) before ranking in select, and add `lo` to the excluded interfaces. Update the ranking_and_lan test so it no longer expects 127.0.0.1 in published.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Demonstrated by the code and its own test: a loopback address is included in the published list. Confirm with a test that select() on a candidate set containing 127.0.0.1 omits it from published.

scanner_findings.title: Refusal replies disclose the server's configured capacity to any remote peer
scanner_findings.prerequisites: A remote peer sends an upload or download that exceeds a limit or finds all slots busy. The reply is sent over the stream to that peer.
scanner_findings.impact: Each refusal reveals the exact max_transfer_size, max_transfers and max_transfer_time of the listener to whoever asks. That is more than a refused peer needs to know, and it helps a peer probe capacity or tune a flood to just under the busy threshold. It is a mild information disclosure, not a secret leak.
scanner_findings.evidence: Line 219-221: `"too_large" => format!("refused reason=too_large max_bytes={}", limits.max_transfer_size)`; line 223: `"busy" => format!("refused reason=busy max_transfers={}", limits.max_transfers)`. These strings are sent via inc.respond at line 345 and recv.stop at line 340.
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Send only the reason code to remote peers (for example `refused reason=busy`) and keep the configured numbers in the local log event. Keep the detail only if the documented protocol in docs/cli-events.md requires it.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Hypothesis that the numbers are a meaningful disclosure. Whether the protocol needs them is not visible in the supplied source, so check docs/cli-events.md and the bench client.

scanner_findings.title: Instance identifier and endpoint ID are echoed to every requesting peer
scanner_findings.prerequisites: Any remote peer sends an echo request, which is answered with the `me` prefix built from the endpoint ID and the process instance ID.
scanner_findings.impact: If the instance ID is meant to be process-local or private, every peer that sends a request learns it, and can link it across requests or to the node's other activity. The endpoint ID is public anyway, so the risk depends entirely on what instance_id represents, which is not in the supplied source.
scanner_findings.evidence: Line 78: `let instance = hex::encode(ep.instance_id());` and line 82: `let me = format!("endpoint={endpoint_id} instance={instance}");`, then line 178-181: `let reply = format!("{me} to={to} from={from} echo={}", ...)`.
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: If instance_id is not intended for peers, omit it from the reply and keep it in local logs only. If it is intended to be public, document that in the reply format.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Needs the definition of ep.instance_id() in golem-p2p (not supplied). Treat as a hypothesis until its meaning is confirmed.

scanner_findings.title: A member can grow retained link history without bound by reporting fresh peer IDs
scanner_findings.prerequisites: An attacker holds one valid membership certificate, so it is a member of the closed network. It can then report one signed report every 4 s (the default min_interval), each listing up to 256 connections with peer IDs it invents. Generating valid node IDs is cheap.
scanner_findings.impact: Each tick copies every link of every online or stale node into the 5 s sample and the 1-minute aggregate, and both are kept for the full retention (7 days by default). Peers that do not report are never checked, and distinct link keys are never capped. A single member that rotates peer IDs adds up to 256 new link keys per report, so the retained history and minutes-*.jsonl files grow linearly with time for the whole retention window. Memory and disk use are therefore bounded only by time, not by the number of members or by MAX_NODES. Only the rate limit (about 1 report per 4 s) and the 256-connection cap apply.
scanner_findings.evidence: tick(): `for l in &links { ... s.links.insert(format!("{},{}", l.a, l.b), LinkSample { ... }) }` at lines 693-709. merged_links() adds every connection of every non-offline node: `for c in &n.report.connections { if c.peer == *id { continue; } ... views.entry(key).or_default().push(View { ... }) }` at lines 588-602. validate() only parses c.peer as NodeId (lines 352-363) and does not cap distinct peers. push_minute() keeps the aggregate for the full retention window (lines 737-744).
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Store only links whose both ends are known nodes, or only links with at least one reporting end that is currently online. Cap the number of link keys per sample and per minute, and drop links that are not reported by a node that is itself a known member. Consider a global cap on links per sample, with an explicit overflow counter.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Demonstrated by code reading, not by a run. A test should send reports with 256 fresh peer IDs per report for a few simulated minutes and measure the size of the minutes-*.jsonl files and the in-memory minutes deque. The impact magnitude is a hypothesis until measured.

scanner_findings.title: Signature and certificate work runs under the global mutex before any rate limit
scanner_findings.prerequisites: Anyone who can reach POST /v1/report, which is the one route meant to be public. Requests may carry arbitrary headers and bodies of up to 64 KiB. No authentication is needed to reach the verification step.
scanner_findings.impact: Every request reaches verify() before any rate limit. verify() hashes the body with SHA-256 and recovers the signer, then decodes and checks the certificate. All of this runs while holding the single std Mutex that also protects the dashboard, state, history, metrics and the sampler. The handler is async but locks a blocking std Mutex, so a burst of invalid requests can hold up tokio worker threads and delay every other request and the sampler. Axum sets no concurrency limit here, so the number of parallel requests is not capped by the code.
scanner_findings.evidence: async fn report: `let r = s.lock().expect("poisoned").accept(&body, &headers, now_ms());` (lines 1395-1398). accept_inner runs `golem_p2p::telemetry::verify(...)` on the full body (lines 471-477) before the bucket check (lines 508-521). Only the body size check comes before it (lines 462-464).
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Move the rate-limit check and cheap header and size checks before any signature work, keyed by the signature's claimed key bytes or by client address at the proxy. Do the crypto outside the lock, and lock only to read and write node state. Use tokio's async Mutex or a dedicated blocking task, and add a concurrency limit on the report route.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Hypothesis. A test should send a flood of 64 KiB requests with invalid signatures and measure lock hold time and the latency of GET /metrics during the flood. The Prometheus and dashboard routes are not in the supplied files for their auth configuration.

scanner_findings.title: A long history query aggregates all retained minutes under the global mutex
scanner_findings.prerequisites: Anyone who can reach GET /v1/history. The collector applies no authentication itself (the docs say to put it behind a proxy). The range parameter is clamped only to the retention, which defaults to 7 days.
scanner_findings.impact: A request with range=604800 (or any range up to retention) makes history() walk every retained minute sample, aggregate them in groups, and build a per-group BTreeMap of every link. The work is proportional to retained minutes times links per sample, and it runs while holding the global mutex that the report handler and the sampler also need. The answer is capped at 720 points, but the work is not. Repeated requests cost the server about this much each time, and nothing is cached.
scanner_findings.evidence: history handler: `let range = Duration::from_secs(range.clamp(60, max));` then `let v = c.history(now_ms(), range, node, link)` while holding `c` (lines 1449-1458). history(): `for s in self.minutes.iter().filter(|s| s.t >= since) { ... out.push(aggregate(&group, group_t.expect("set"), step)); ... }` (lines 939-950). aggregate() builds a `BTreeMap<String, ...>` of all links for each group (lines 1234-1256).
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Cache the aggregated series per range, or precompute coarser tiers at sample time. Do the aggregation without holding the mutex (copy the needed samples out first). Add a limit on concurrent history queries, and cap the number of links in aggregates (see the previous finding).
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Hypothesis. A benchmark with 7 days of synthetic minute samples and a realistic link count, measuring time per GET /v1/history?range=604800 and the lock hold time, would confirm or refute it.

scanner_findings.title: Replay protection state is saved only once a minute and at shutdown, so a crash reopens the replay window
scanner_findings.prerequisites: The collector process dies without a graceful shutdown (crash, OOM, kill -9) and restarts from nodes.json. The attacker holds a previously accepted signed report of a member, with its signature and certificate headers, from a source they can observe. Reports are only refused as replays when their timestamp is not newer than the stored last_ts_ms.
scanner_findings.impact: After the restart, last_ts_ms is up to about a minute older than the last accepted report. Any captured report whose timestamp falls inside that gap, and within the 5 min clock skew, is accepted again. This inflates the delta counters that feed network totals and the per-node rate and counts. It does not forge membership.
scanner_findings.evidence: Accept path: 'if prev.is_some_and(|p| report.ts_ms <= p.last_ts_ms) { return Err(refuse(StatusCode::CONFLICT, "replay")); }' and the stored state: 'last_ts_ms: report.ts_ms'. Persistence happens only in push_minute ('self.save_nodes();' at line 753, reached once per minute of samples) and at shutdown ('shared.lock().expect("poisoned").save_nodes();' in run). A crash between these points loses last_ts_ms for every node that reported in that window.
scanner_findings.suggested_fix: Persist last_ts_ms (and the bucket) on every accepted report, or write nodes.json atomically with each accept and before responding 204. Alternatively reject any report whose ts_ms is not greater than the newest timestamp seen in the store's last write plus a margin. Add a test that restarts the collector without save_nodes and replays a report.
scanner_findings.validation_needed: Hypothesis. Write a test that accepts a report, drops the Collector without calling save_nodes, reopens from the store, and checks whether the same report is accepted. The code path is clear, but whether a crash reopens the window in practice depends on the deployment's restart behaviour.

scanner_findings.title: Read routes (state, nodes, history, metrics, dashboard) have no authentication in the router
scanner_findings.prerequisites: The collector is reachable beyond localhost and the proxy in front of it does not protect the GET routes. The module docs and the --listen default say to add authentication in front, so this depends on deployment. Nothing in the source enforces it.
scanner_findings.impact: Anyone who can reach the listener can read node IDs, node names, versions, commits, OS and arch, relay URLs, the peer graph of the network, NAT booleans, lifetime counters and link history, with no membership proof. This is information disclosure about a closed network, not a write.
scanner_findings.evidence: '.route("/v1/report", post(report).layer(DefaultBodyLimit::max(MAX_REPORT_SIZE)))' followed by '.route("/", get(dashboard))', '.route("/v1/state", get(state))', '.route("/v1/history", get(history))', '.route("/metrics", get(metrics))' with no auth extractor or middleware. The docs say: 'Only the report route is meant to be public; put the others behind authentication'.
